articles.title: Governments and experts gather in Nairobi to tackle the global housing crisis
articles.summary: A home is a place where people can feel safe. Yet billions worldwide do not have a proper place to live. As the global housing crisis deepens, government representatives and housing experts are gathering at the United Nations in Nairobi from 26-27 November to discuss how to address it.
articles.content:
For many people living in informal settlements, the housing crisis goes hand in hand with the climate crisis.

“People don’t sleep at night because they don't know if their houses will be standing the next day,” said Anacláudia Rossbach, Executive Director of UN-Habitat, the agency working to make cities more sustainable, which is hosting the meeting.

The objective is to better understand the scale and nature of homelessness, improve national housing policies, and ensure that housing can withstand growing environmental and climate pressures.

This is the third session of the Open-ended Intergovernmental Expert Working Group on Adequate Housing for All (OEWG-H) which was established in 2023. It aims to advance a comprehensive set of recommendations for the UN-Habitat Assembly in 2029.

Speaking to UN News ahead of the meeting, Ms. Rossbach emphasized the importance of bringing the housing crisis to the attention of Member States and building consensus on how to address it.

UNICEF/Jannatul Mawa

Putting homelessness on the agenda

Adequate housing means having the right to live somewhere in security, peace and dignity. For example, people should not fear being evicted, or that their home is unsafe because it was built with the wrong materials. She also highlighted the need to put homelessness on the global housing agenda.

“We estimate that we have about 300 million people living without a roof over their heads, but we don't have a global definition of homelessness,” she said.

Having this definition means that people who are experiencing homelessness can be more easily included in housing policies in line with internationally agreed targets.

However, having a home does not necessarily mean that it is safe. The latest UN-Habitat World Cities Report estimates that up to 3.4 billion people lack adequate housing, with more than 1.1 billion living in informal settlements and slums. This usually entails a lack of secure tenure, sanitation or safe water.

As governments face the challenge of improving existing housing and building new homes, they must also consider the environmental consequences of construction and where these homes are built. “Housing is the cornerstone for adaptation,” she stressed.

Soundcloud

Shaping policies with communities

To address the housing crisis, an essential component remains listening to those most affected. Ms. Rossbach underscored the importance of involving local authorities and communities in the development of housing policies, especially those in more vulnerable positions. Local governments, she explained, are closer to the communities they serve and are therefore better positioned to understand their needs.

From communities and local governments to researchers and the private sector, efforts to address housing challenges are already underway. “They are finding solutions. They are innovating, and they are moving the frontier,” she said.

At the meeting, UN-Habitat will launch the first version of its Housing Knowledge Platform, bringing together housing data, policy resources and examples of practices from around the world.

Despite the magnitude of the global housing crisis, Ms. Rossbach finds hope in the solutions already emerging on the ground.

“The decisions here, they will have a direct impact on the lives of people,” she said. “So, let's keep people at the centre of our minds this week.”

articles.personality_title: Global leaders meet in Nairobi to improve housing for billions
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many people around the world do not have safe or stable homes. This problem is connected to climate change and affects billions of people, especially those living in informal settlements or slums.

**What happened** – From November 26 to 27, government representatives and housing experts gathered at the United Nations meeting in Nairobi, Kenya. The meeting was hosted by UN-Habitat, an agency focused on making cities better places to live. They discussed how to understand homelessness better, improve housing policies, and make homes stronger against environmental threats.

**Impact** – This meeting is part of a new working group created in 2023 to find solutions for adequate housing worldwide. It is important because it aims to create clear definitions of homelessness and build better rules to protect people’s right to a safe home. The meeting also launched a new Housing Knowledge Platform to share data and examples from around the world, helping countries learn from each other.

**What's next step** – The group will continue working on recommendations to present at the UN-Habitat Assembly in 2029. They plan to involve local communities and governments more, listening closely to those affected to create better housing policies.

**One-sentence takeaway** – International leaders and experts are joining forces in Nairobi to create practical steps toward safe and secure housing for billions of people worldwide.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des dirigeants mondiaux se réunissent à Nairobi pour améliorer le logement de milliards de personnes
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Beaucoup de personnes dans le monde n'ont pas de maisons sûres ou stables. Ce problème est lié au changement climatique et touche des milliards de personnes, surtout celles vivant dans des établissements informels ou des bidonvilles.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Du 26 au 27 novembre, des représentants gouvernementaux et des experts en logement se sont réunis lors d'une réunion des Nations Unies à Nairobi, au Kenya. Cette réunion était organisée par ONU-Habitat, une agence qui travaille à rendre les villes meilleures. Ils ont discuté de la meilleure compréhension de l'itinérance, de l'amélioration des politiques de logement, et de la construction de maisons plus résistantes aux menaces environnementales.

**Impact** – Cette réunion fait partie d'un nouveau groupe de travail créé en 2023 pour trouver des solutions à un logement adéquat dans le monde. Elle est importante car elle vise à créer des définitions claires de l'itinérance et à établir de meilleures règles pour protéger le droit à un logement sûr. La réunion a également lancé une nouvelle Plateforme de Connaissances sur le Logement pour partager des données et des exemples du monde entier, aidant ainsi les pays à apprendre les uns des autres.

**Prochaine étape** – Le groupe continuera à travailler sur des recommandations à présenter à l'Assemblée ONU-Habitat en 2029. Ils prévoient d'impliquer davantage les communautés locales et les gouvernements, en écoutant attentivement les personnes concernées pour créer de meilleures politiques de logement.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des dirigeants et experts internationaux unissent leurs forces à Nairobi pour créer des mesures concrètes en faveur d’un logement sûr et sécurisé pour des milliards de personnes dans le monde.
articles.personality_title_es: Líderes mundiales se reúnen en Nairobi para mejorar la vivienda de miles de millones
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchas personas en el mundo no tienen hogares seguros o estables. Este problema está relacionado con el cambio climático y afecta a miles de millones de personas, especialmente a quienes viven en asentamientos informales o barrios pobres.

**Qué pasó** – Del 26 al 27 de noviembre, representantes gubernamentales y expertos en vivienda se reunieron en una sesión de las Naciones Unidas en Nairobi, Kenia. La reunión fue organizada por ONU-Hábitat, una agencia que trabaja para mejorar las ciudades. Discutieron cómo entender mejor la falta de vivienda, mejorar las políticas de vivienda y hacer que los hogares sean más resistentes a las amenazas ambientales.

**Impacto** – Esta reunión forma parte de un nuevo grupo de trabajo creado en 2023 para encontrar soluciones para una vivienda adecuada en todo el mundo. Es importante porque busca crear definiciones claras de la falta de vivienda y establecer reglas para proteger el derecho a un hogar seguro. También se lanzó una nueva Plataforma de Conocimiento sobre Vivienda para compartir datos y ejemplos de todo el mundo, ayudando a los países a aprender entre sí.

**Próximo paso** – El grupo seguirá trabajando en recomendaciones para presentar en la Asamblea de ONU-Hábitat en 2029. Planean involucrar más a las comunidades y gobiernos locales, escuchando atentamente a quienes están afectados para crear mejores políticas de vivienda.

**Mensaje en una frase** – Líderes y expertos internacionales se unen en Nairobi para crear pasos prácticos hacia viviendas seguras y protegidas para miles de millones de personas en todo el mundo.

articles.title: ICC: Promote, Protect International Justice
articles.summary:
Click to expand Image
          



  
        
  

        
                      
      
        
              Seventeenth session of the International Criminal Court's Assembly of States Parties in The Hague, Netherlands, December 2018. 

                    © 2018 Syd Boyd/Coalition for the International Criminal Court
          
    


  
The upcoming session of the International Criminal Court’s (ICC) annual Assembly of States Parties takes place as the court and the broader international justice system face unrelenting pressure from the United States.Offering the US government solutions that would hollow out the court’s mandate and guarantee impunity for certain powerful individuals would severely undermine the legitimacy and credibility of the ICC and the international justice system.Member countries of the ICC should focus on safeguarding the court’s independence and taking concrete actions to protect the court and those cooperating with it.(The Hague) – Member countries of the International Criminal Court (ICC) should prioritize measures to promote and protect the court and those cooperating with it, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today. The 24-page report makes detailed recommendations for the annual session of the ICC’s Assembly of States Parties, which will convene in The Hague from November 30 to December 7, 2026.This year’s session takes place as the court and the broader international justice system face unrelenting pressure from the United States. On October 9, the US government escalated its campaign to destroy the ICC “brick by brick” by imposing sanctions on the whole court under a February 2025 executive order. This followed the sanctioning of ICC judges and prosecutors, a United Nations human rights expert, and three leading Palestinian rights organizations. Yet, the ICC continues to advance its critical work for justice. The landmark trial of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte is scheduled to begin on November 30.“The start of the Duterte trial at the same time as the annual ICC Assembly session should remind member countries of the court’s critical importance,” said Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch. “At the session, member countries should stand firmly by the court and not take steps that could curtail victims’ access to justice.”In his October 9 announcement, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated the sanctions were aimed at shielding US nationals from investigation and prosecution at the ICC. The Trump administration has previously objected to the court’s investigation of Israeli nationals for their conduct in Palestine. The ICC has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for serious crimes in Gaza. After a China-Russia-US summit––at which the three countries’ leaders adopted a declaration that included expressing concern for state consent and the immunity of state officials, and that the ICC and other similar bodies should not “abuse their jurisdiction”––US President Donald Trump on November 20 remarked that Russian President Vladimir Putin “especially is not happy with” the ICC. Putin faces war crimes charges before the ICC for the unlawful deportation and forcible transfer of children from occupied areas of Ukraine to Russia. The US government has pitched the court-wide sanctions as “structured ... to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address” its “concerns.” The authorization of certain transactions with the court for a six-month period, which otherwise would have been immediately affected by the court-wide sanctions, is an ultimatum to member countries to meet the US government’s demands; but these demands effectively allow the Trump administration to determine whom the court can prosecute, Human Rights Watch said. In the lead-up to the Assembly session, media reports referred to concerning proposals by some countries to meet US demands, including curbing the court’s jurisdiction over nationals of nonmember countries or exempting heads of state from the court’s reach. Offering the US government solutions that would hollow out the court’s mandate and guarantee impunity for certain powerful individuals would severely undermine the legitimacy and credibility of the ICC and the international justice system, Human Rights Watch said.At the Assembly session, ICC member countries should focus on safeguarding the court’s independence and taking concrete actions to protect the ICC and those cooperating with it. This should include calling on the European Union to urgently activate its Blocking Statute, which aims to shield European operators from the effects of extraterritorial sanctions, Human Rights Watch said.Seven lawsuits have been brought in US federal court over the US sanctions targeting the ICC and those supporting its work. Human Rights Watch, together with three other human rights organizations, filed one of these lawsuits on August 11, seeking to have the sanctions regime struck down. A wide range of human rights organizations, other experts, and former US government officials have filed amicus (friend of the court) briefs in support of the suit.The United States is also stepping up diplomatic pressure on ICC member countries to leave the court. Over the past year, seven countries—Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali, Venezuela, Chad, Naoero and Tajikistan—decided to withdraw from the ICC. While not all of these withdrawals can be linked to US pressure, they undermine efforts to achieve the global adoption of the court’s founding treaty, the Rome Statute. Tajikistan’s notification of withdrawal on November 20 followed its failure, for a second time, to arrest Putin when he was visiting the country and surrender him to the court, as required by its obligations as an ICC member. The Tajik parliament had adopted legislation on withdrawal in October.“US efforts to press countries to withdraw from the Rome Statute are both an attack on states that have chosen to become ICC members and on international justice itself,” Evenson said. “The Trump administration has little standing with respect to either.”At the upcoming session, ICC members should call on the countries that have withdrawn to reconsider their decisions and remain part of the court. They should also engage with other ICC members to develop strategies to counter US pressure and promote a unified community of member countries, Human Rights Watch said.Other issues on the Assembly’s agenda include electing 6 of the court’s 18 judges and making decisions on the process for the election of the court’s next prosecutor, expected to be held in December 2027. On July 24, 2026, the Assembly removed ICC Prosecutor Karim Khan from office for serious misconduct and serious breach of duty. Member countries should focus on merit and the most qualified candidates as they make decisions about elections that will shape the future of the court, Human Rights Watch said.“The ICC’s daily work as grave abuses continue around the world is proof of the urgent need to protect the global rule of law,” Evenson said. “Member countries should demonstrate that they reject the idea of a world where might makes right and use their annual meeting to stand for ensuring no one is above the law.”
articles.content:
Click to expand Image Seventeenth session of the International Criminal Court's Assembly of States Parties in The Hague, Netherlands, December 2018. © 2018 Syd Boyd/Coalition for the International Criminal Court

The upcoming session of the International Criminal Court’s (ICC) annual Assembly of States Parties takes place as the court and the broader international justice system face unrelenting pressure from the United States.

Offering the US government solutions that would hollow out the court’s mandate and guarantee impunity for certain powerful individuals would severely undermine the legitimacy and credibility of the ICC and the international justice system.

Member countries of the ICC should focus on safeguarding the court’s independence and taking concrete actions to protect the court and those cooperating with it.

(The Hague) – Member countries of the International Criminal Court (ICC) should prioritize measures to promote and protect the court and those cooperating with it, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today. The 24-page report makes detailed recommendations for the annual session of the ICC’s Assembly of States Parties, which will convene in The Hague from November 30 to December 7, 2026.

This year’s session takes place as the court and the broader international justice system face unrelenting pressure from the United States. On October 9, the US government escalated its campaign to destroy the ICC “brick by brick” by imposing sanctions on the whole court under a February 2025 executive order. This followed the sanctioning of ICC judges and prosecutors, a United Nations human rights expert, and three leading Palestinian rights organizations. Yet, the ICC continues to advance its critical work for justice. The landmark trial of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte is scheduled to begin on November 30.

“The start of the Duterte trial at the same time as the annual ICC Assembly session should remind member countries of the court’s critical importance,” said Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch. “At the session, member countries should stand firmly by the court and not take steps that could curtail victims’ access to justice.”

In his October 9 announcement, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated the sanctions were aimed at shielding US nationals from investigation and prosecution at the ICC. The Trump administration has previously objected to the court’s investigation of Israeli nationals for their conduct in Palestine. The ICC has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for serious crimes in Gaza.

After a China-Russia-US summit––at which the three countries’ leaders adopted a declaration that included expressing concern for state consent and the immunity of state officials, and that the ICC and other similar bodies should not “abuse their jurisdiction”––US President Donald Trump on November 20 remarked that Russian President Vladimir Putin “especially is not happy with” the ICC. Putin faces war crimes charges before the ICC for the unlawful deportation and forcible transfer of children from occupied areas of Ukraine to Russia.

The US government has pitched the court-wide sanctions as “structured ... to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address” its “concerns.” The authorization of certain transactions with the court for a six-month period, which otherwise would have been immediately affected by the court-wide sanctions, is an ultimatum to member countries to meet the US government’s demands; but these demands effectively allow the Trump administration to determine whom the court can prosecute, Human Rights Watch said.

In the lead-up to the Assembly session, media reports referred to concerning proposals by some countries to meet US demands, including curbing the court’s jurisdiction over nationals of nonmember countries or exempting heads of state from the court’s reach. Offering the US government solutions that would hollow out the court’s mandate and guarantee impunity for certain powerful individuals would severely undermine the legitimacy and credibility of the ICC and the international justice system, Human Rights Watch said.

At the Assembly session, ICC member countries should focus on safeguarding the court’s independence and taking concrete actions to protect the ICC and those cooperating with it. This should include calling on the European Union to urgently activate its Blocking Statute, which aims to shield European operators from the effects of extraterritorial sanctions, Human Rights Watch said.

Seven lawsuits have been brought in US federal court over the US sanctions targeting the ICC and those supporting its work. Human Rights Watch, together with three other human rights organizations, filed one of these lawsuits on August 11, seeking to have the sanctions regime struck down. A wide range of human rights organizations, other experts, and former US government officials have filed amicus (friend of the court) briefs in support of the suit.

The United States is also stepping up diplomatic pressure on ICC member countries to leave the court. Over the past year, seven countries—Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali, Venezuela, Chad, Naoero and Tajikistan—decided to withdraw from the ICC. While not all of these withdrawals can be linked to US pressure, they undermine efforts to achieve the global adoption of the court’s founding treaty, the Rome Statute. Tajikistan’s notification of withdrawal on November 20 followed its failure, for a second time, to arrest Putin when he was visiting the country and surrender him to the court, as required by its obligations as an ICC member. The Tajik parliament had adopted legislation on withdrawal in October.

“US efforts to press countries to withdraw from the Rome Statute are both an attack on states that have chosen to become ICC members and on international justice itself,” Evenson said. “The Trump administration has little standing with respect to either.”

At the upcoming session, ICC members should call on the countries that have withdrawn to reconsider their decisions and remain part of the court. They should also engage with other ICC members to develop strategies to counter US pressure and promote a unified community of member countries, Human Rights Watch said.

Other issues on the Assembly’s agenda include electing 6 of the court’s 18 judges and making decisions on the process for the election of the court’s next prosecutor, expected to be held in December 2027. On July 24, 2026, the Assembly removed ICC Prosecutor Karim Khan from office for serious misconduct and serious breach of duty. Member countries should focus on merit and the most qualified candidates as they make decisions about elections that will shape the future of the court, Human Rights Watch said.

“The ICC’s daily work as grave abuses continue around the world is proof of the urgent need to protect the global rule of law,” Evenson said. “Member countries should demonstrate that they reject the idea of a world where might makes right and use their annual meeting to stand for ensuring no one is above the law.”

articles.personality_title: International Criminal Court members unite to defend justice amid pressure
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The International Criminal Court (ICC) is a global court that tries people accused of serious crimes like war crimes and crimes against humanity. It faces strong pressure from the United States, which has imposed sanctions and pushed some countries to leave the court. The ICC’s annual meeting of member countries will take place in The Hague from November 30 to December 7, 2026.

**What happened** – Ahead of this meeting, Human Rights Watch released a report urging ICC members to protect the court’s independence. The US government recently sanctioned the entire court and some of its officials, aiming to stop investigations involving US nationals. Despite this, the ICC is moving forward with important cases, including the trial of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte starting November 30. Some countries have suggested changes that would limit the court’s power, but Human Rights Watch warns these would weaken justice.

**Impact** – The ICC is one of the few places where powerful leaders can be held accountable for serious crimes. Pressures and sanctions threaten to make the court less effective and could allow some leaders to avoid punishment. The court’s work helps victims get justice and supports international rules that no one is above the law. Protecting the ICC ensures that serious crimes do not go unpunished.

**What's next step** – During the Assembly session, member countries will discuss how to keep the court independent and protect those who work with it. They will also elect six judges and plan for the election of the next prosecutor in 2027. Human Rights Watch encourages members to reject demands that limit the court’s reach and to ask countries that left the ICC to return. Legal cases are ongoing in US courts to challenge the sanctions.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Despite political pressure and sanctions, ICC member countries are preparing to defend the court’s role in delivering justice for serious crimes and protecting the rule of law worldwide.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les membres de la Cour pénale internationale unis pour défendre la justice face aux pressions
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La Cour pénale internationale (CPI) est un tribunal mondial qui juge les personnes accusées de crimes graves comme les crimes de guerre et les crimes contre l’humanité. Elle fait face à de fortes pressions des États-Unis, qui ont imposé des sanctions et poussé certains pays à quitter la Cour. La réunion annuelle des membres aura lieu à La Haye du 30 novembre au 7 décembre 2026.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Avant cette réunion, Human Rights Watch a publié un rapport demandant aux membres de la CPI de protéger l’indépendance de la Cour. Le gouvernement américain a récemment sanctionné la Cour entière et certains de ses responsables pour empêcher les enquêtes impliquant des ressortissants américains. Malgré cela, la CPI avance dans des procès importants, dont celui de l’ancien président philippin Rodrigo Duterte qui commence le 30 novembre. Certains pays ont proposé des changements qui limiteraient le pouvoir de la Cour, mais Human Rights Watch avertit que cela affaiblirait la justice.

**Impact** – La CPI est l’un des rares lieux où les dirigeants puissants peuvent être tenus responsables de crimes graves. Les pressions et sanctions menacent de rendre la Cour moins efficace et pourraient permettre à certains leaders d’échapper à la justice. Le travail de la Cour aide les victimes à obtenir justice et soutient les règles internationales affirmant que personne n’est au-dessus des lois. Protéger la CPI garantit que les crimes graves ne restent pas impunis.

**Prochaines étapes** – Pendant la session de l’Assemblée, les membres discuteront de la façon de préserver l’indépendance de la Cour et de protéger ceux qui y collaborent. Ils éliront aussi six juges et prépareront l’élection du prochain procureur en 2027. Human Rights Watch encourage les membres à rejeter les demandes qui limitent la portée de la Cour et à inviter les pays qui l’ont quittée à revenir. Des actions en justice sont en cours aux États-Unis pour contester les sanctions.

**Une phrase clé** – Malgré les pressions politiques et les sanctions, les membres de la CPI se préparent à défendre le rôle de la Cour pour rendre justice dans les crimes graves et protéger l’état de droit dans le monde.
articles.personality_title_es: Miembros de la Corte Penal Internacional se unen para defender la justicia ante presiones
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La Corte Penal Internacional (CPI) es un tribunal mundial que juzga a personas acusadas de crímenes graves como crímenes de guerra y crímenes contra la humanidad. Enfrenta una fuerte presión de Estados Unidos, que ha impuesto sanciones y ha presionado a algunos países para que salgan de la Corte. La reunión anual de los países miembros se realizará en La Haya del 30 de noviembre al 7 de diciembre de 2026.

**Qué pasó** – Antes de esta reunión, Human Rights Watch publicó un informe pidiendo a los miembros de la CPI que protejan la independencia de la Corte. El gobierno estadounidense sancionó recientemente a toda la Corte y a algunos de sus funcionarios para detener investigaciones que involucren a ciudadanos estadounidenses. A pesar de esto, la CPI continúa con casos importantes, incluido el juicio del expresidente filipino Rodrigo Duterte, que comienza el 30 de noviembre. Algunos países han propuesto cambios que limitarían el poder de la Corte, pero Human Rights Watch advierte que esto debilitaría la justicia.

**Impacto** – La CPI es uno de los pocos lugares donde los líderes poderosos pueden ser responsabilizados por crímenes graves. Las presiones y sanciones amenazan con hacer que la Corte sea menos efectiva y podrían permitir que algunos líderes evadan el castigo. El trabajo de la Corte ayuda a las víctimas a obtener justicia y apoya las reglas internacionales que dicen que nadie está por encima de la ley. Proteger la CPI asegura que los crímenes graves no queden impunes.

**Próximo paso** – Durante la sesión de la Asamblea, los miembros discutirán cómo mantener la independencia de la Corte y proteger a quienes trabajan con ella. También elegirán a seis jueces y planificarán la elección del próximo fiscal en 2027. Human Rights Watch anima a los miembros a rechazar demandas que limiten el alcance de la Corte y a pedir a los países que salieron de la CPI que regresen. Se están llevando a cabo demandas legales en Estados Unidos para impugnar las sanciones.

**Una frase clave** – A pesar de la presión política y las sanciones, los miembros de la CPI se preparan para defender el papel de la Corte en brindar justicia por crímenes graves y proteger el estado de derecho en todo el mundo.
